result:
There's a word—coined, not official—for the sudden awareness that every stranger you pass is living a life as dense and urgent as your own: *sonder*. I think about it most in traffic, honestly. Some Tuesday afternoon, stopped at a light, watching the driver beside me drum fingers on the wheel with an expression of pure preoccupation—and realizing that person is mid-story. Their story began decades before mine intersected with it and will continue long after. They were a child once. They have a photo somewhere they keep meaning to frame. Someone, possibly, loves them in ways that are complicated and imperfect and real.

What gets me isn't just the volume of it—it's the opacity. We move past hundreds of interiors daily without a glimpse inside. Every car a sealed novel. Every train window framing someone reviewing a conversation from three years ago, composing an apology, rehearsing joy or grief so thoroughly practiced it's invisible.

And yet occasionally there's a leak. A woman laughing alone at her phone. A man standing in his yard, staring upward at nothing weather-related. A kid pressing their face against a bus window as though glass might dissolve if belief were strong enough. These leaks feel almost scandalous—unauthorized proof of inner life.

Maybe that's why we stare, why gossip exists, why stories matter at all. Fiction is formalized window-peeping. Art is a stranger saying: here, I'll show you mine.

The light changes. The drummer drives off into their own vast, unwitnessed plot. I drive into mine.
